name: Spreader grafts
lead: Spreader grafts are thin strips of cartilage, usually taken from the nasal septum, that surgeons place between the septum and the upper lateral cartilages during rhinoplasty. For appearance, they help keep the sides of the nasal bridge straight and evenly wide after a dorsal hump has been lowered, so the bridge reads as a smooth line from forehead to tip rather than pinched or crooked. They are also used to widen the internal nasal valve, which supports breathing [1][2][9].

Lowering a hump often disrupts the junction of the septum and upper lateral cartilages (the keystone area), and surgeons describe spreader grafts, spreader flaps and dorsal-preservation methods as three families of approaches for rebuilding or avoiding that disruption [1][12][14]. Spreader grafts and flaps are described as among the most commonly used midvault techniques in rhinoplasty [13].

Research on spreader grafts includes a number of small randomized trials and a systematic review of 40 studies on complications. Trials comparing grafts with no grafts, with autospreader flaps and with dorsal preservation have generally found that all approaches improve breathing and appearance, with some differences in patient satisfaction and in nasal-valve measurements [17][18][19][20][21].

paras: The internal nasal valve is the narrowest part of the nasal airway, bounded by the septum and the caudal edge of the upper lateral cartilage. Surgeons have long investigated valve incompetence as a contributor to airway obstruction alongside septal deviation [4][5]. A spreader graft is a rectangular cartilage strip fixed on one or both sides of the dorsal septum so that the upper lateral cartilages are held apart from it [9].

Variants described in the literature include alar spreader grafts, proposed for a pinched nasal tip [6], the upper lateral splay graft [7], and the spreader flap, in which the upper lateral cartilage itself is folded inward rather than a separate graft being used [3][8]. General rhinoplasty references also note that spreader grafts, often combined with flaring sutures, are used when the internal valve is too narrow [9].

The spreader graft was introduced in the 1980s as a way to reconstruct the roof of the middle nasal vault after rhinoplasty, and later papers extended the idea: alar spreader grafts for a pinched tip (1992) [6], the upper lateral splay graft (1998) [7], and the spreader flap, which folds the patient's own upper lateral cartilage inward in place of a separate graft (2007) [8].

Component dorsal hump reduction, described in 2004, emphasized preserving the dorsal aesthetic lines and reducing how often grafts are needed in primary operations [2]. More recent literature has turned toward dorsal preservation, in which the bony and cartilaginous dorsum is lowered without cutting the keystone area, including the push-down technique reassessed in 2018 and the modified Skoog method, in which the removed dorsal segment is reshaped and replaced so that it acts as an onlay spreader graft [1][16]. Reviews describe the open-versus-endonasal approach, donor sites such as rib cartilage, and filler use as other open questions in primary rhinoplasty alongside spreader grafts and autospreader flaps [12].

Spreader grafts are used to treat nasal obstruction attributed to internal valve narrowing or collapse. A cadaver and clinical study of surgery for the dysfunctional nasal valve reported outcomes of valve-directed procedures [5], and a study of 160 primary and secondary rhinoplasty patients compared the relative contribution of septal and valve surgery to airway improvement [4].

After hump reduction, surgeons use grafts or flaps to avoid an inverted-V deformity, dorsal irregularities, and a narrowed middle vault, and the surgeon who described component dorsal reduction notes that preserving the upper lateral cartilages can reduce how often spreader grafts are needed in primary cases [2]. They are also used in correcting a crooked nose, where straightening the septum and dorsum is a recurring difficulty and revision rates are described as fairly high [10].

In an open or closed rhinoplasty the surgeon harvests a septal strip, or uses ear or rib cartilage if septal cartilage is insufficient, shapes it into a narrow rectangular piece, and fixes it along one or both sides of the dorsal septum beneath the upper lateral cartilages [9][12]. Surgeons choose between unilateral and bilateral placement, longer or shorter grafts, and grafts that extend toward the tip, depending on the anatomy [12][14].

Autospreader flaps are an alternative in which the upper lateral cartilages are folded in rather than a separate cartilage piece used; flaring and advancement variants of spreader flaps have also been described for reconstructing the internal valve [8][23]. The nasal-valve literature describes grafts as one option among several structural and suture-based maneuvers [15].

Dorsal preservation techniques aim to lower the dorsum without removing the hump and cutting the keystone area. One surgeon's series of 320 cases over five years described a push-down technique and noted that most conventional reduction operations destroy the keystone area and therefore require reconstruction [1]. Spreader flaps are presented as an alternative that uses the patient's own upper lateral cartilage [8].

A systematic review and case series of rhinoplasty in adults over 55 describes internal and external valve collapse and a worsening dorsal hump as part of the aging nose, which are among the problems addressed with structural grafting in that population [22]. Revision rhinoplasty and posttraumatic noses are other settings in which spreader grafts are reported [10][12].

A randomized trial of 50 patients in Brazil (published in The Laryngoscope in 2025; registered as NCT04499469) allocated people undergoing reduction septorhinoplasty to spreader grafts or none. Quality-of-life scores (NOSE-p, ROE and a nasal obstruction visual analog scale) improved after surgery in both groups, with no significant difference between them at 6 or 12 months [18][3].

A double-blind randomized study of 30 septorhinoplasty patients compared surgery with and without spreader grafts and reported significant differences favoring grafts in a visual analog scale and in acoustic rhinometry measurements (minimal cross-sectional area and volume on the left side), leading the authors to conclude that grafts may help prevent internal valve narrowing [17]. A 40-patient randomized study of deviated noses treated with osteotomies and septoplasty with or without spreader grafts found improvements in both groups and higher satisfaction with appearance and breathing in the graft group [21].

A randomized study of 48 patients compared autospreader flaps with spreader grafts: nasal airflow improved in both groups, olfaction was similar, and satisfaction was higher with autospreader flaps [20]. An 84-patient randomized trial comparing dorsal preservation with conventional hump reduction plus spreader flap reconstruction found no significant differences at one year in residual hump, width, projection, rotation or patient-reported scores [19]. A second registered trial compared a spreader graft with a lateral crural overlay technique [11].
Earlier work includes a 160-patient study of septal versus valve surgery for airway improvement [4] and a cadaver and clinical analysis of valve surgery [5].

A 2022 systematic review of 40 studies reported that common complications with spreader grafts included persistent nasal obstruction, inverted-V deformity, open roof deformity, deviation and infection, with pooled revision rates of 0.62 percent for spreader grafts and 0.35 percent for spreader flaps and no significant difference in complication rates between the methods [13]. Reviews of dorsal hump reduction describe a nontrivial revision rate for hump surgery in general and recommend reconstructing the midvault at the first operation [14].

Grafts are placed as part of rhinoplasty, which carries general surgical risks; general references report revision in roughly 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasties and swelling that can take a year or more to resolve [9].

Spreader grafts are one component of a wider rhinoplasty toolkit that includes hump reduction, osteotomies, septoplasty, tip grafts and dorsal augmentation with cartilage or fascia, sometimes combined in a single operation [9][12].

card.summary: Cartilage strips placed beside the septum to open the internal nasal valve and keep the nose bridge straight after hump reduction; supported mainly by surgeon case series.
card.note: Part of rhinoplasty; revision surgery is reported in roughly 5 to 20 percent of rhinoplasties.

quick.overview:
Spreader grafts are small strips of cartilage, usually from the septum, placed along the nasal bridge during rhinoplasty. Surgeons use them to widen the internal nasal valve, keep the bridge straight and avoid a pinched mid-nose after a hump is reduced.
The evidence is mostly surgeon case series and technique papers, with a few registered trials.
quick.mechanism: The graft holds the upper lateral cartilages away from the septum, widening the angle of the internal nasal valve and preserving smooth dorsal lines.
quick.risks: It is done under general rhinoplasty risks, and revision rhinoplasty accounts for roughly 5 to 20 percent of cases. It is a surgical procedure performed only by clinicians.
